name: Hubble’s 1929 distance–velocity relation
description: Hubble analyzed a relation between estimated extragalactic distances and radial velocities in a sample of nebulae.

date.basis: Year is the date of the described episode in the cited source, not necessarily the invention or first conception.

events.statement: Hubble published a distance–radial velocity analysis using individual objects and grouped data.

evidence.supports: 1929 paper compares 24 individual distances with radial velocities, also grouped as 9 groups.
Describes sample-specific slope estimates and earlier contributions including Slipher, Lemaître and Robertson.

contributions.resource: Analyzed and published the distance–velocity comparison.

evidence.supports: 1929 paper compares 24 individual distances with radial velocities, also grouped as 9 groups.

contributions.resource: Earlier measurements of radial velocities used in Hubble’s analysis.

evidence.supports: Identifies Slipher as the source of most Doppler shifts used by Hubble.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest episode established from the sources collected for this scoped record, not a claim of global priority.

caveats: Slipher supplied many underlying velocities and Lemaître and others published earlier related work. Hubble’s slope is a historical sample-dependent estimate, not a modern expansion-rate measurement.

research.note: Independent second reading checked the dated event evidence and cited quantitative measures; other facets remain as previously assessed. people.note: Earlier velocity measurements used in Hubble’s 1929 analysis.

measures.subject: Hubble’s fit to 24 individual nebulae as reported by Way
measures.conditions: Approximately 465 ± 50 km/s/Mpc in the 1929 individual-object solution, reported by Way; the plus/minus is the historical quoted uncertainty, not a modern measurement or a specified confidence interval.

evidence.supports: Describes sample-specific slope estimates and earlier contributions including Slipher, Lemaître and Robertson.

measures.subject: Hubble’s 1929 sample with individual estimated distances
measures.conditions: 24 individual objects; the alternative fit grouped them into nine groups.

evidence.supports: 1929 paper compares 24 individual distances with radial velocities, also grouped as 9 groups.

links.statement: Hubble’s extragalactic distance work used the period–luminosity relation identified by Leavitt and later calibrated by others.

evidence.supports: The Harvard account connects Leavitt’s relation with Hubble’s later distance and expansion work.
